name: Reproductive value theory (face score)

lead: Reproductive value theory, as discussed in looksmaxxing, is the idea that the traits judged attractive, especially in faces, act as signals of health, youth and fertility, so a face score reflects reproductive potential. Within this view a lower score is read as a signal of less favourable genes, and a higher one the opposite.

For people trying to improve their looks, the framework is a way of explaining why features such as symmetry, youthful skin and averageness matter, and so which of them to work on. Researchers describe these as proposed explanations and note criticisms, including cultural variation and mixed evidence on links to actual health.

paras: People apply it by rating faces (a 'face score') and reading the result through an evolutionary lens, then focusing on features thought to signal health and youth such as skin quality, symmetry and facial proportions.

The framework is interpretive. Critics in the research literature say links between attractive features and real health are questioned and that preferences vary across cultures, so treating a score as a verdict on someone's genes is contested.

angle.text: The framework is used to explain why certain facial features count as attractive and which to improve. It guides attention toward skin, symmetry, youthfulness and averageness.

lead: Reproductive value is a term used in social psychology for the reproductive capacity and potential reproductive success of female humans, and also for the traits people judge when choosing partners [1]. A separate sense in population genetics refers to an individual's expected contribution to future generations [2].

In looksmaxxing discussion the two ideas are combined into the claim that a face's attractiveness score reflects underlying reproductive potential, so a low score signals less desirable genes. The motivation is practical: if attractiveness works as a signal of health and youth, improving the features that carry that signal, such as skin condition and facial balance, is a route to looking better.

Wikipedia's article on physical attractiveness describes evolutionary explanations along these lines, including that attractiveness may signal fertility and health, that symmetry may signal genetic health, and that youthful features are favoured in female faces. It also lists criticisms, such as questions about links to actual health, cultural variation in preferences and small or biased samples [3].

paras: Social-psychology usage defines reproductive value as female humans' reproductive capacity and potential reproductive success, and as the attributes assessed in mate selection [1]. The population-genetics usage refers to an individual's contribution to future generations [2].

Proponents of the framework draw on evolutionary explanations of attraction. As summarised in Wikipedia, attractiveness is thought to signal fertility and health, symmetry may signal good inheritance and fewer developmental disturbances, youthful features are favoured because of the fertility they imply, and averaged faces are often rated as more attractive [3].

The same account lists limits. Some researchers question the link between attractive features and actual health, one report found absolute flawlessness can be disturbing, and preferences vary across cultures, including for body fat, femininity and height. Several studies use small or biased samples, and averageness findings come mainly from samples of white women [3]. A 2009 study by Markus Jokela in Evolution and Human Behavior, cited by Wikipedia, examined the link between physical attractiveness and reproductive success in late 20th-century United States data [1].
No studies found testing a face score as a measure of genetic quality or reproductive value.
